newsitem.title: UK: Buybacks back in vogue for British companies.
newsitem.headline: Buybacks back in vogue for British companies.

text.p: Share buybacks are likely to continue apace in Britain as increasingly assertive shareholders insist companies focus on their core businesses, analysts said on Wednesday.
British rental company Thorn Plc announced plans on Wednesday to return 87 million pounds ($140 million) of excess cash to shareholders, some 14 percent of its market value.
Just 24 hours earlier music company EMI Group Plc, demerged from Thorn last year, said it planned to return 500 million pounds to its shareholders.
"We are in an environment where cash is building up and companies are not spending it as aggressively as in the past," said Gary Dugan, an analyst with JP Morgan.
"In the past corporates would go out and buy peripheral businesses rather than focus on the one business," he added.
But the trend away from the conglomerates of the 1990s means shareholders are demanding the return of any cash that a company does not need for its core activities.
"Investors want companies to grow within their own businesses and dominate these," Dugan said.
British companies spent billions of pounds repurchasing shares before the previous Conservative government last October amended tax rules on such schemes.
The Treasury acted to prevent tax-exempt pension funds from claiming back Advance Corporation Tax (ACT) paid by companies on buybacks or special dividends.
The change forced global news and information group Reuters Holdings Plc to put on hold its plans to return 613 million pounds to shareholders by way of a bonus issue of special dividend shares.
Reuters has said that it remains its intention to return cash to shareholders but it is continuing to review its options over the best method to adopt.

Thorn Plc plans to return capital via the issue of "B" shares which the company will offer to repurchase. Shareholders will receive six new ordinary shares and seven B shares for every seven existing ordinary shares.
The method, which corporate financiers at SBC Warburg have developed, has been employed previously by Yorkshire Water Plc and Southern Electric Plc.
It will also provide the basis for the 2.4 billion pound capital return planned as part of the merger of drinks giants Grandmet Plc and Guinness.

Tax experts say the reorganisation of a company's share structure as part of a repurchase removes ACT from the equation. This is because the tax applies only to the additional value on top of a share's original worth.
The net result is that companies are not liable to pay ACT and tax-exempt funds cannot claw it back. Under the Thorn scheme, the purchase proceeds will be subject to UK capital gains tax.

Tax experts believe that Britain's new finance minister Gordon Brown is likely to overhaul the system at some point, but may not move in his first Budget statement as Chancellor, which he is expected to deliver over the next few weeks.
"The government will see some leakage here as companies are not paying ACT," said Robert Turnbull, a tax partner at accountancy group KPMG.
"I think Gordon Brown will tear up the rule book and start again. My best guess is that may happen in a year or so," he said.
